questions.stem: When were dematerialised shares introduced in India?
questions.passage_context:
The journey of Indian capital markets has been transformative. From paper-based trading and a closed system in the 1990s, India now hosts one of the world's most digitized exchanges. The introduction of dematerialised shares in 1996, electronic trading, and rolling settlement transformed market microstructure. SEBI's role as regulator has continually evolved — from prosecuting market manipulators to fostering investor protection.

Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) have been an important source of capital. Yet their inflows are volatile, rising in risk-on global cycles and exiting during crises. Domestic Institutional Investors (DIIs) — mutual funds, insurance companies, pension funds — have grown to provide a counter-balancing stable base. The Mutual Funds industry alone manages assets exceeding ₹50 lakh crore as of 2025, up from ₹10 lakh crore a decade ago.

Retail participation has been the most striking shift. SIP (Systematic Investment Plan) subscriptions exceed ₹20,000 crore monthly. Demat accounts now exceed 15 crore — more than double pre-pandemic levels. The broadening of the investor base has helped buffer the markets against external shocks.

Yet challenges persist. Quality of issuance — particularly in the SME and start-up segments — needs improvement. Investor education must keep pace with market innovation, especially around derivatives, options, and crypto-linked products. SEBI's enforcement capacity is being tested by sophisticated cross-border manipulation. Climate-related disclosure is just beginning to feature in regulatory frameworks.

Looking ahead, three priorities will shape Indian capital markets: deepening corporate bond liquidity, integrating ESG considerations into mainstream investing, and ensuring that retail participation translates into long-term wealth creation rather than speculative loss.
